statement: Four identical printers working together would print a large order in 6 hours. All four start at the same time. After 1 hour, one printer breaks down, and 2 hours after that a second printer breaks down. The two printers that are left finish the order. How many hours after the start is the order finished?

choices.misconception: I ignored the breakdowns and used the time for all four printers working together.
I found how long the last two printers worked on their own and gave that instead of the time from the start.
I thought each printer that breaks down adds a quarter of 6 hours, so I added $1\frac{1}{2}$ hours twice to 6.
I worked out that two printers alone would need 12 hours for the whole order and gave that.

hints: Measure the order in printer-hours: one printer working for one hour.
Four printers for 6 hours is a fixed amount of work. Work out how much is done before each breakdown, then how long two printers need for the rest.
The order is $4 \times 6 = 24$ printer-hours. In the first hour 4 are done, and in the next 2 hours another $3 \times 2 = 6$.

solutions.reliable: The whole order needs $4 \times 6 = 24$ printer-hours. In the first hour four printers do 4 of them. In the next 2 hours three printers do $3 \times 2 = 6$ more, so $24 - 4 - 6 = 14$ printer-hours are left. Two printers do 2 printer-hours every hour, so they need $14 \div 2 = 7$ hours. The order is finished $1 + 2 + 7 = 10$ hours after the start. The transferable idea: when the workers are identical, count the job in worker-hours and subtract as the team changes.
solutions.elegant: Each printer's fair share is a quarter of the order, 6 printer-hours. The first printer to break worked only 1 hour, leaving 5 hours of its share, and the second worked 3 hours, leaving 3. The two survivors split those 8 missing hours, 4 each, so they work $6 + 4 = 10$ hours.

whyOnTest: Work questions reward measuring the job in worker-hours instead of juggling fractions.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
